issues.legal_issue: An unregistered lease instrument cannot establish its contractual terms, but may be considered to determine the nature and character of possession.
material_facts: The parties executed an indenture for a lease exceeding one year, but the indenture was not registered.
The tenant’s written statement separately admitted that it occupied the property under the lease for a fixed term and that the term had expired.
issues.conclusion: The contents of the unregistered indenture were inadmissible to determine the lease’s contractual terms; the indenture could be considered only to assess the nature and character of possession.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 107 of the Transfer of Property Act 1882 and 17 and 49 of the Registration Act 1908 require registration of a lease for a term exceeding one year and render an unregistered instrument inadmissible to prove the terms of the transaction, subject to its use for a collateral purpose such as assessing the nature and character of possession. The Court applied Satish Chand Makhan v Govardhan Das Byas, (1984) 1 SCC 369, and distinguished Park Street Properties Private Limited v Dipak Kumar Singh, (2016) 9 SCC 268, which recognizes that tenancy may be determined from other evidence, including the parties’ conduct.

predicates.civil_suit_concerning_possession: A civil suit concerns recovery of possession of property occupied by a person under an alleged lease.
predicates.lease_term_exceeds_one_year: The alleged lease is for a term exceeding one year.
predicates.lease_instrument_unregistered: The instrument recording the alleged lease was not registered.

issues.definition: When a possession suit concerns an unregistered instrument for a lease exceeding one year, the instrument cannot prove its contractual terms but may be considered to assess the character of possession.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord need not give a termination notice when a tenant who entered under a lease admits that its fixed term expired and remains in possession thereafter.
material_facts: The tenant entered into possession under a lease for a fixed term.
In its written statement, the tenant expressly admitted that the lease term had expired while it remained in occupation.
The landlord brought a suit for possession after the admitted expiry of the term.
issues.conclusion: The lease determined by efflux of time, leaving the tenant in possession as a tenant at sufferance; no termination notice was necessary, and the suit for possession was maintainable.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 111(a) of the Transfer of Property Act 1882, a lease determines by efflux of the time limited by it. A tenant who entered lawfully but remains in possession after the lease has ended is a tenant at sufferance, and no notice under Section 106 is necessary to recover possession. The Court relied on R V Bhupal Prasad v State of A P, (1995) 5 SCC 698, and distinguished Satish Chand Makhan v Govardhan Das Byas, (1984) 1 SCC 369, where the tenant had not admitted the alleged fixed term and was held to be a tenant holding over under Section 116. It also distinguished Park Street Properties Private Limited v Dipak Kumar Singh, (2016) 9 SCC 268. The Court cited Nopany Investments (P) Ltd v Santokh Singh (HUF), (2008) 2 SCC 728, for the proposition that filing an eviction suit is itself notice to quit under the general law.

rule.if: eviction_suit_for_possession and tenant_entered_under_lease and tenant_admitted_fixed_term_expired and tenant_remained_in_possession_after_expiry

predicates.eviction_suit_for_possession: A landlord brings a suit seeking possession from a person occupying the property.
predicates.tenant_entered_under_lease: The occupant originally obtained possession lawfully under a lease.
predicates.tenant_admitted_fixed_term_expired: The occupant expressly admitted that the fixed term of the lease had expired.
predicates.tenant_remained_in_possession_after_expi: The occupant continued in possession after the admitted expiry of the lease without a renewed lease.

issues.definition: When a landlord sues for possession against a person who entered under a lease, admits that its fixed term expired, and remains in possession afterward, no termination notice is required and the possession suit is maintainable.
